JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)  -- South Africa has refused the Dalai Lama a visa to attend an international peace conference in Johannesburg this week, a presidential spokesman said. The Tibetan spiritual leader and Nobel Laureate did not receive a visa because it was not in South Africa's interest for him to attend, said Thabo Masebe. South Africa thinks that, if the Dalai Lama attended the conference, the focus would shift away from the 2010 World Cup -- the global soccer championship it will host next year. "We cannot allow focus to shift to China and Tibet," Masebe said, adding that South Africa has gained much from its trading relationship with China. De Klerk said that the decision to refuse the visa made a "mockery" of the peace conference. "The decision to exclude the Dalai Lama is irreconcilable with key principles on which our society is based including the principles of accountability, openness and responsiveness and the rights to freedom of expression and free political activity," he said. "South Africa is a sovereign constitutional democracy and should not allow other countries to dictate to it regarding who it should, and should not admit to its territory - regardless of the power and influence of the country." A representative of the Dalai Lama said he was not surprised by the decision. The Tibetan government in exile thinks that China has pressured many countries to refuse a visit by the Dalai Lama, according to Chhime Chhoekyapa, an aide in Dharamsala, India. The Dalai Lama fled China in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule. The peace conference was billed as an opportunity to showcase South Africa's role as a human-rights champion ahead of its hosting of soccer's World Cup next year. It was to bring together Noble Laureates and top soccer officials. In addition to Tutu and De Klerk, laureates Nelson Mandela and Martti Ahtisaari, Sepp Blatter, president of soccer's international governing body, and actress Charlize Theron were invited to attend. The event had the blessing of the Nobel Committee.

**South Africa Bars Dalai Lama From Nobel Peace Conference, Stirring Debate Over China’s Influence Ahead of 2010 World Cup**

*Johannesburg* — South Africa’s refusal to allow the Dalai Lama to enter the country for a Nobel-backed peace conference has triggered an international dispute, drawing criticism from human rights advocates and fellow Nobel laureates who say Pretoria bowed to pressure from China ahead of the 2010 FIFA World Cup.

The Tibetan spiritual leader had been invited to attend a peace conference in Johannesburg alongside several prominent Nobel Peace Prize laureates, including Archbishop Desmond Tutu and former South African President F.W. de Klerk. The gathering was intended to promote peace, reconciliation and the role of sport in uniting divided societies, with South Africa preparing to host the World Cup the following year.

But South African officials declined to grant the Dalai Lama a visa, saying his presence would divert attention from the country’s World Cup preparations and broader national interests. The decision prompted outrage among organizers and invited participants, several of whom withdrew in protest. The conference was ultimately postponed.

Archbishop Tutu, one of South Africa’s most respected moral voices and a longtime supporter of the Tibetan cause, sharply criticized the government’s decision, calling it a betrayal of the country’s democratic values. De Klerk also pulled out, saying the refusal undermined the purpose of the event.

The controversy placed South Africa in an uncomfortable spotlight: a nation celebrated for overcoming apartheid and championing human rights was now accused of silencing a globally recognized religious leader to avoid offending Beijing.

### Government Cites “National Interest”

South African officials denied that the decision was the result of direct pressure from China, but they acknowledged that the timing of the visit was sensitive. Government representatives argued that the conference, if dominated by the politics of Tibet, could distract from the promotion of South Africa as host of the 2010 World Cup — the first to be held on the African continent.

“The world’s attention should be on South Africa and the World Cup,” officials said in defending the decision. They insisted the Dalai Lama was not being permanently barred from the country, but that the moment was inappropriate.

Critics found that explanation unconvincing. To many observers, the move appeared to reflect China’s growing economic and diplomatic influence across Africa, including in South Africa, the continent’s largest economy at the time and an increasingly important trade partner for Beijing.

China had become a major investor in African infrastructure, mining, energy and telecommunications. South Africa, rich in minerals and seeking expanded markets and investment, had cultivated close ties with Beijing. The two countries had also aligned in several multilateral forums, emphasizing sovereignty, development and opposition to Western dominance in global politics.

### Beijing’s Longstanding Objection to the Dalai Lama

China regards the Dalai Lama as a separatist and strongly objects to foreign governments granting him high-profile visits or official recognition. Beijing has repeatedly pressured countries to avoid meetings with him, arguing that Tibet is an inseparable part of China and that engagement with the exiled leader interferes in Chinese domestic affairs.

The Dalai Lama, who fled Tibet in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule, has lived in exile in India for decades. He remains the most prominent international symbol of Tibetan identity and Buddhist spirituality. Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989, he has advocated what he calls a “Middle Way” approach, seeking genuine autonomy for Tibet within China rather than full independence.

Chinese authorities reject that position, accusing him of disguising separatist aims. Beijing says its rule has brought modernization, development and improved living standards to Tibet. Tibetan exiles and rights groups counter that China has suppressed religious freedom, restricted Tibetan language and culture, and maintained tight political control over the region.

Tibet has been a particularly sensitive issue for China since the 2008 unrest in Lhasa and other Tibetan areas, when protests turned violent and were followed by a major security crackdown. Those events occurred months before the Beijing Olympics, intensifying international scrutiny of China’s human rights record.

### A Blow to South Africa’s Moral Image

For South Africa, the visa decision carried special symbolic weight. The country’s transition from apartheid to democracy was widely viewed as a moral triumph, and leaders such as Nelson Mandela and Tutu became global icons of reconciliation and justice. Because the peace conference was associated with Nobel laureates and themes of nonviolence, barring the Dalai Lama struck many critics as especially contradictory.

Tutu, who had frequently warned South Africa’s post-apartheid leaders against abandoning human rights principles, said the decision suggested the government was placing economic interests above moral obligations.

Human rights groups echoed that view, arguing that South Africa’s foreign policy had increasingly shifted from the values-based diplomacy of the Mandela era toward a more pragmatic approach centered on trade, alliances and geopolitical influence.

The African National Congress-led government had often emphasized solidarity with developing nations and respect for sovereignty. But critics said that stance sometimes translated into silence on abuses committed by powerful allies.

### China’s Expanding Role in Africa

The dispute also highlighted a broader trend: China’s expanding presence across Africa and its ability to shape diplomatic behavior far beyond its borders.

By the late 2000s, China had become one of Africa’s most important economic partners. It offered loans, built roads, railways and stadiums, purchased natural resources and deepened ties with governments through high-level summits and investment deals. Unlike many Western donors, Beijing generally avoided public criticism of domestic governance issues, making it an attractive partner for many African states.

In return, China expected support — or at least silence — on issues it defined as core national interests, including Taiwan, Tibet and Xinjiang. Countries that hosted the Dalai Lama often faced formal protests from Beijing, and in some cases diplomatic or economic retaliation.

South Africa’s decision therefore fed perceptions that China’s economic weight was altering the diplomatic calculations of even countries with strong human rights traditions.

### Conference Collapses After Boycott

The peace conference had been intended to bring together Nobel laureates, political leaders and sports figures to discuss how football and global sporting events could promote peace. But after the visa decision, several key participants withdrew, saying the event could not credibly proceed while one invited Nobel laureate was excluded.

Organizers postponed the gathering, a public embarrassment for South Africa as it sought to project openness and global leadership before the World Cup.

The episode also raised questions about the role of FIFA and global sport in political controversies. Although the conference was not a FIFA event, it was tied to the broader international attention surrounding South Africa’s World Cup preparations. The government’s claim that the Dalai Lama’s presence would distract from the tournament only deepened debate over whether major sporting events encourage governments to suppress controversy rather than confront it.

### A Lasting Diplomatic Controversy

The visa refusal became one of several incidents in which South Africa faced criticism over its handling of the Dalai Lama. In later years, similar disputes would arise when the Tibetan leader sought to visit the country for events involving Archbishop Tutu, reinforcing concerns that Pretoria was unwilling to risk angering Beijing.

For supporters of the Dalai Lama, the South African decision was a clear example of China exporting its Tibet policy through diplomatic pressure. For China and its allies, it was a matter of respecting sovereignty and avoiding support for what Beijing sees as separatism.

For South Africa, the controversy exposed a difficult balancing act: preserving its post-apartheid reputation as a defender of human dignity while navigating a world in which economic power increasingly shapes political choices.

As the country prepared to welcome millions of football fans in 2010, the dispute served as a reminder that global sporting spectacles do not exist apart from international politics. Even a conference dedicated to peace could become entangled in one of the world’s most sensitive geopolitical conflicts.
